I will keep to the system I trust most on my land in Quzhou County: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is what fits our climate, my age, my labor capacity, and the way water and machinery are used here. I do not want a complicated planting structure this year. Wheat and maize are the crops I know best, they sell easily, and I can manage them with familiar timings. I will use improved wheat seed for stable tillering and disease resistance, and hybrid maize seed because hybrid maize usually gives me better yield and stronger stand. I will keep fertilizer at a moderate level instead of chasing the highest possible yield, because input costs matter and I would rather aim for a steady harvest than take extra risk. For wheat, I will do rotary tillage before sowing, apply base fertilizer, irrigate at key stages like overwintering recovery, jointing, and grain filling if water allows, and spray only when weeds, aphids, or disease pressure justify it. After wheat harvest, I will move quickly into summer maize, using the remaining moisture and keeping the turnaround short. For maize, I will use lighter tillage, focus nitrogen more heavily than phosphorus and potassium, irrigate mainly at the critical vegetative and silking stages, and control weeds and insects with limited sprays. This is the simplest and most reliable annual plan for me, and it matches how I would protect labor, cost, and yield on my farm.
